Axios Future of Defense
By Colin Demarest · Oct 07, 2026

Hello from New York City. God bless Amtrak.

  • Headed to AUSA next week? Give us a shout!
  • I'll be there Oct. 12. Thomas will be there Oct. 13-14.

⚓ Situational awareness: Anduril Industries will construct Arsenal-2 in Baltimore County, Maryland. Parts for Virginia-class submarines are expected to be built at the mega-shipyard, which is backed by almost $4 billion in private capital. President Trump spoke about it yesterday afternoon.

Can't stop won't stop: Talking to tanks, questioning Golden Dome and landing F-16s in Taiwan.

Today's newsletter is 1,784 words, a 6.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Sixth-gen monopoly
 

A conceptual look at F/A-XX. Photo: Courtesy of Boeing
 

The future of American fighter aircraft is now Boeing's to decide.

The big picture: The world's sixth-largest defense contractor by revenue has secured a monopoly on these sixth-generation warplanes, with the rights to build not only the U.S. Air Force's F-47 but also the Navy's F/A-XX.

Driving the news: Analysts I spoke with described this moment as an upswing for Boeing, which has taken lumps on the VC-25B presidential transporter, KC-46 refueler and T-7 trainer.

  • "This is, obviously, a huge, huge win," Eli Cook, a senior associate at the Capstone strategy firm, told me. "It's a clean sweep."
  • "Modern, next-generation aircraft — especially combat aircraft, with all the systems and subsystems and weapons, etc. — are extremely hard to pull together in an effective way," he added.

Here are some things to chew on:

💳 The "full-scale development" contract for F/A-XX is worth more than $20 billion. It includes multiple aircraft for ground and weapons integration testing, among other trials.

🚫 Boeing declined to say how many aircraft are actually due, whether there will be different versions or variants for testing purposes, by when they must be furnished, and what other companies it is in talks with. Boeing also did not share specs, such as range and payloads.

🗓️ Both the program and deal were long awaited. That ostensibly provided plenty of time to mature designs, invest in infrastructure and identify potential pitfalls.

📴 The contract rollout, itself, was muted. A few paragraphs and X posts shared. No Oval Office ceremony with big, illustrative boards.

🔎 The render, which should be treated with skepticism, shows a very broad, flat, tailless aircraft with chunky landing gear. It also appears there is a single person in the cockpit.

🖼️ The render is reminiscent of a photo taken aboard the USS Theodore Roosevelt in 2018.

🆕 F/A-XX will augment and replace F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers beginning in the 2030s, according to the Pentagon.

🔥 The propulsion has not been disclosed, but has been described as a derivative of an existing engine. A GE Aerospace spokesperson told me the company is "excited to see this important program advance."

🔁 F/A-XX will operate alongside Lockheed Martin's F-35C, the carrier variant, as well as Collaborative Combat Aircraft. (Boeing was one of several aerospace companies selected by the Navy last year to cook up "conceptual designs" for the service's robo-wingmen.)

♻️ There will be common DNA between F/A-XX and F-47. Both will be stealthy, for example. Beyond that, little authoritative information is available.

What they're saying: "The long-overdue final downselect for the F/A-XX program is great news for the U.S. aircraft carrier fleet," Rep. Joe Courtney (D-Conn.) said in a statement.

  • The warplane, he added, "will serve as a critical platform for the Navy to overcome the tyranny of distance in the Indo-Pacific region."

Zoom out: On the same day it won the F/A-XX contest, Boeing also secured a $2.4 billion contract for more F-15EX fighters.

  • A total 120 F-15EX are under contract for the Air Force.

The bottom line: "The good news is, overall, there's been a real focus on building a lot of capacity," Jerry McGinn, an industrial base expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told me.

  • "Now they've got to be able to execute. That's always the trick."

2. Exclusive: Enter Ibex
 

The Ibex autonomous ground vehicle. Photo: Courtesy of Overland AI
 

Overland AI this morning will debut Ibex, an autonomous ground vehicle capable of shuttling thousands of pounds of materiel and designed for rapid relocation aboard V-22 Ospreys.

Why it matters: The Seattle startup is building the reconfigurable robo-resupplier for the Marine Corps as well as the Army and Special Operations Command.

The big picture: Ibex has been in design since the beginning of the year, Overland AI co-founder Greg Okopal told me. Two prototypes are undergoing daily tests in central Washington. Some tweaks and refinements are expected ahead of production later this year.

  • More than a dozen AGVs are on order, via a nearly $20 million APFIT contract with the Marine Corps ground-based air-defense shop and a previously unreported $4.5 million add-on that brings in the 75th Ranger Regiment.
  • "We are a very field-forward, field-testing-focused company," Okopal said.
  • "If you're going to deliver these vehicles to a unit, it needs to keep up with what they are doing," he said. "It cannot slow them down."

Zoom in: Ibex is based on a Polaris MRZR Alpha, a platform also tapped for the Corp's Ultra-Light Tactical Vehicle. It can carry 2,000 pounds, hit speeds greater than 35 mph and cruise for 250 miles. It's fueled by diesel or JP-8.

  • "It's narrower, it's longer, but otherwise pretty close in scale to what an Ultra is," Okopal said, referencing the startup's other AGV.
  • "It's a lot of payload space, a lot of payload capacity," he added. "You can add sensors. You can add effectors."

Context: Ibex will initially be used to restock Marine Air Defense Integrated Systems, which are used for counter-drone and overhead defense. Overland AI teased that application over the summer — but kept the actual vehicle under wraps.

The bottom line: "We can use roads, if they're there. But we do not need roads. We can move through the most challenging terrain that is out there," Okopal said.

  • "And we go fast."

3. Siri but deadly
 

Soldiers conduct live-fire training with an M2 Bradley at Fort Irwin, California, in 2022. Photo: Hunter Xue/DVIDS
 

Near-future versions of General Dynamics' next-generation tank and XM30 combat vehicle could have voice controls onboard, letting crews manipulate sensors, radios, drones and more with plain English instructions.

Why it matters: Such a setup could simplify training, ease troop burdens and improve battlefield performance — or what the military so coyly calls lethality.

Driving the news: General Dynamics Land Systems and Primordial Labs today announced a "master teaming agreement," after years of working together.

  • The former makes heavy-duty, household-name vehicles, like the Abrams and Stryker. The latter makes a locally operating human-machine interface known as Anura.
  • I gave Anura a go early last year, orchestrating small drones in a field in Virginia.

What they're saying: "I'm tracking that this is a first-of-its-kind effort to put this on ground combat vehicles in the U.S. Army," GDLS director of strategy Geoff Norman, the former head of the Next Generation Combat Vehicles Cross-Functional Team, told me.

  • "We do think this is going to result in more-rapid crew functions, inside the vehicle."

Zoom in: Anura-enabled voice controls are anticipated for future upgrade packages, according to Norman. The idea, he said, "is to spin the capability into future model years, as we really gain the insights from soldier experiments and soldier feedback."

Zoom out: This is a perfect example of big working with little, and vice versa.

  • General Dynamics is the third-largest defense contractor in the world by revenue. Primordial disclosed a seed round, led by Squadra Ventures, in 2023.
  • "We're along for the ride on multiple GDLS platforms," Primordial CEO Lee Ritholtz told me.

4. Golden questions
By Thomas Novelly
 

Illustration: Natalie Peeples/Axios
 

Top senators are questioning the effectiveness and cost of President Trump's Golden Dome missile defense effort.

Why it matters: Trump's sprawling plan is still failing to win needed support from lawmakers — and it's in dire financial straits.

State of play: Lawmakers and defense analysts said during a Sept. 29 Senate Armed Services subcommittee hearing they're in the dark about Golden Dome's technology and capabilities.

  • Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said given various cost estimates it appeared that nationwide missile coverage was "not in the cards" and wondered "who is protected and who isn't?"
  • A spokesperson for the Defense Department's Golden Dome office declined to comment.

By the numbers: In May, the Congressional Budget Office estimated the missile shield could cost as much as $1.2 trillion over 20 years.

  • Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) told a CBO official during last week's hearing she wanted "more informed analysis in the future."

Yes, but: David Mosher, CBO's national security analysis director, told lawmakers CBO received its first briefing from the Golden Dome office just five days before the Sept. 29 hearing.

  • Gen. Michael Guetlein, Golden Dome's program manager, has decried the CBO estimate and said the system will remain within a $185 billion budget.

Follow the money: Golden Dome's been funded exclusively through reconciliation, a maneuver that allows the Republican majority to pass additional spending.

  • It netted $24.4 billion last year, and almost all of the $17.5 billion requested for the program this year comes from reconciliation.
 
 
5. Quick hits
 

Touchdown in Taiwan. Photo: Wang Jinfu/Taiwan Military News Agency
 

🇹🇼 The first batch of Lockheed Martin F-16 Block 70s arrived in Taiwan, the island's military announced. The new-build jets landed near Taitung, a city on the southeastern side of the island.

  • Why it matters: This is just the beginning. Additional aircraft are expected soon, according to Defense Minister Wellington Koo.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: This is good news for Taiwan — especially as 2027 nears.

🚀 The U.S. Army selected Anduril Industries, Castelion, Lockheed Martin, Mach Industries and RTX to prototype the Precision Strike Missile Increment 4. Fly-offs are planned.

  • Why it matters: The missiles are expected to be able to hit moving land and sea targets at ranges greater than 620 miles.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: That's roughly doubling PrSM's range, as Inside Defense pointed out.

📈 Northrop Grumman's self-funded YFQ-48A flew autonomously for the first time, executing taxi, takeoff, in-flight maneuvers and landing in Mojave, California.

  • Why it matters: "Talon Blue's first flight is one step toward a new generation of autonomous capabilities," Northrop's Craig Woolston said in a statement. "Every flight and lesson strengthens our broader autonomy work and sharpens what comes next."
  • 💭 My thought bubble: I was one of a lucky few who attended the Talon unveiling in December. More on that here.
